da-2026-da-43.approach: Reduce every statement to the definition $\chi^2_k = $ sum of squares of $k$ independent standard normals, plus two facts: $\chi^2_2 = \text{Exp}(\text{mean } 2)$ and $\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ for normal samples.
concepts: Sample variance of a normal sample (Cochran)

steps.title: Option (A): sum of n squared standard normals
steps.body: By definition, if $Z_1,\ldots,Z_k$ are i.i.d. $N(0,1)$ then $\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i^2 \sim \chi^2_k$. Here $k = n$, so $\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i^2 \sim \chi^2_n$. **(A) correct.**

steps.title: Option (B): deviations from the sample mean
steps.body: For an i.i.d. $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ sample, $\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2} = \frac{\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ (and it is independent of $\bar X$). With $\sigma^2 = 1$: $\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$. One degree of freedom is lost because the $n$ deviations satisfy the linear constraint $\sum (X_i - \bar X) = 0$. **(B) correct.**

steps.title: Option (C): two squared normals give an exponential
steps.body:
$X_1^2 + X_n^2 \sim \chi^2_2$ (two independent standard normals). The $\chi^2_k$ density is that of $\text{Gamma}\left(\frac{k}{2}, \text{scale } 2\right)$; for $k=2$ it is $\text{Gamma}(1, 2)$:
$$f(y) = \tfrac12 e^{-y/2},\quad y > 0,$$
which is the exponential density with mean $2$ (rate $\tfrac12$). Also $E[\chi^2_2] = 2$. **(C) correct.**

steps.title: Option (D): the squared standardised mean
steps.body: $\bar X \sim N\left(0, \frac{1}{n}\right)$ because $\text{Var}(\bar X) = \frac{1}{n^2}\cdot n\cdot 1 = \frac1n$. Hence $\sqrt n\,\bar X \sim N(0,1)$ — a **single** standard normal — and $(\sqrt n\,\bar X)^2 \sim \chi^2_1$, not $\chi^2_2$. **(D) incorrect.**

optionAnalysis.reason: Sum of squares of $n$ independent $N(0,1)$ variables is $\chi^2_n$ by definition.
Standard result for normal samples: $\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$; the constraint $\sum(X_i-\bar X)=0$ removes one degree of freedom.
$\chi^2_2$ has density $\frac12 e^{-y/2}$, i.e. exponential with mean 2.
$\sqrt n\,\bar X$ is one standard normal, so its square is $\chi^2_1$; "2 degrees of freedom" is wrong.

da-2026-da-43.shortcut: Count independent standard normals being squared: $n$ in (A), $n-1$ effective in (B), $2$ in (C) ($\chi^2_2 \equiv$ Exp(mean 2)), and just $1$ in (D).
pitfalls: Thinking $\chi^2_2$ and the exponential are different families — $\chi^2_2$ is exactly Exp with mean 2.
Forgetting the $\sqrt n$ standardisation makes $\sqrt n\,\bar X$ a single $N(0,1)$, giving 1 (not 2) degree of freedom.
Using $n$ instead of $n-1$ degrees of freedom in (B).
da-2026-da-43.verification: Means check: $E[\chi^2_k] = k$. (A) $E\sum X_i^2 = n$ ✓; (B) $E\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2 = (n-1)\sigma^2 = n-1$ ✓; (C) $E[X_1^2+X_n^2] = 2$ = mean of Exp(mean 2) ✓; (D) $E[n\bar X^2] = n\cdot\frac1n = 1 \ne 2$ ✗.

da-2026-da-44.approach: Check each statement against the three defining properties of any CDF — non-decreasing, limits $0$ and $1$, right-continuous — plus the fact that a discrete variable puts positive mass $P(X=a) = F(a) - F(a^-)$ at its support points.

steps.title: (A) positive everywhere? No
steps.body: $F(x) = P(X \le x) \ge 0$, and $\lim_{x\to-\infty} F(x) = 0$. For example, for $X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.5)$, $F(x) = 0$ for all $x < 0$. So $F$ is **non-negative**, not always positive. **(A) false.**

steps.title: (B) non-decreasing: yes
steps.body: If $x_1 < x_2$ then $\{X \le x_1\} \subseteq \{X \le x_2\}$, so $F(x_1) \le F(x_2)$. **(B) true.**

steps.title: (C) jump discontinuity: yes
steps.body:
A discrete $X$ has some value $a$ with $P(X = a) > 0$. Then
$$F(a) - \lim_{x\to a^-}F(x) = P(X = a) > 0,$$
so $F$ jumps at $a$: the CDF is a step function. **(C) true.**

steps.title: (D) left-continuous? No — right-continuous
steps.body: Every CDF is **right**-continuous: $\lim_{x\to a^+}F(x) = F(a)$, because $\{X\le a+\tfrac1k\}\downarrow\{X\le a\}$. At a jump point the left limit is $F(a) - P(X=a) \ne F(a)$, so $F$ is not left-continuous there. **(D) false.**

optionAnalysis.reason: $F(x) = 0$ to the left of the smallest support point (e.g. $x<0$ for a Bernoulli), so it is non-negative, not positive.
$\{X\le x_1\}\subseteq\{X\le x_2\}$ for $x_1<x_2$ — monotonicity of probability.
At each mass point the jump size is $P(X=a) > 0$; a discrete CDF is a step function.
CDFs are right-continuous; at a jump the left limit is $F(a)-P(X=a) \ne F(a)$.

da-2026-da-44.shortcut: $F(x) = P(X \le x)$ with "$\le$" includes the point itself, so the value at a jump belongs to the right piece — right-continuous, not left.
pitfalls: Confusing "positive" with "non-negative".
Mixing up left/right continuity; it would be left-continuous only under the alternative convention $F(x) = P(X < x)$, which GATE does not use.
da-2026-da-44.verification: Bernoulli(0.5): $F = 0$ on $(-\infty,0)$, $0.5$ on $[0,1)$, $1$ on $[1,\infty)$ — non-decreasing, zero on the left, jumps at 0 and 1, and the filled dots sit on the right pieces (right-continuous).

da-2026-da-45.approach: Ridge regression adds $\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2$ to the data loss. Compute the prediction, the MAE on this single instance, the squared-L2 penalty, and add.

steps.title: Data loss (MAE on one instance)
steps.body: $\text{MAE} = \lvert y_{pred} - y_{true}\rvert = \lvert 5 - 3\rvert = 2$.

steps.title: Ridge penalty
steps.body: Ridge uses the squared L2 norm: $\lVert w\rVert_2^2 = (-3)^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$, so the penalty is $\lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2 = 0.20 \times 25 = 5$.

steps.title: Overall regularised loss
steps.body: $L = \text{MAE} + \lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2 = 2 + 5 = 7.00$.

pitfalls: Using $\lVert w\rVert_2 = 5$ instead of $\lVert w\rVert_2^2 = 25$ gives $3$ — ridge penalises the **squared** norm.
Using the L1 norm ($\lvert -3\rvert + 4 = 7$, lasso) gives $2 + 1.4 = 3.4$.
Squaring the error (MSE) instead of taking its absolute value gives $4 + 5 = 9$.
da-2026-da-45.verification: Units check: both terms are plain numbers on this instance; $2 \le L$ and the penalty $5$ dominates because $\lVert w\rVert$ is large — consistent with $7$.

da-2026-da-46.approach: In a fully-connected network without biases, each pair of consecutive layers of sizes $a$ and $b$ contributes an $a\times b$ weight matrix. Sum $a\cdot b$ over consecutive layers.
da-2026-da-46.given: Layers: input $30$ → hidden-1 $4$ → hidden-2 $3$ → output $1$; no biases.

steps.title: Input → hidden layer 1
steps.body: Every one of the $30$ inputs connects to each of the $4$ neurons: $30 \times 4 = 120$ weights.

steps.title: Hidden 1 → hidden 2 → output
steps.body: $4 \times 3 = 12$ weights, then $3 \times 1 = 3$ weights.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $120 + 12 + 3 = 135$ learnable parameters (biases would have added $4 + 3 + 1 = 8$ more; they are excluded).

pitfalls: Adding biases (would give 143) although the question excludes them.
Counting neurons (38) instead of connections.
Treating the input layer as having learnable weights of its own.

da-2026-da-47.approach: Bayes' theorem: $P(D\mid +) = \frac{P(+\mid D)P(D)}{P(+\mid D)P(D) + P(+\mid D^c)P(D^c)}$. A two-level probability tree gives both terms at once.

steps.title: Total probability of a positive test
Apply Bayes
steps.body:
$$P(D\mid +) = \frac{0.24}{0.31} = \frac{24}{31} \approx 0.7742$$
Rounded to two decimals: **0.77**.

da-2026-da-47.shortcut: Think of 100 people: 30 diseased → 24 test positive; 70 healthy → 7 test positive. Of 31 positives, 24 are diseased: $24/31 \approx 0.77$.
pitfalls: Answering $P(+\mid D) = 0.80$ (confusing the direction of conditioning).
Forgetting the false positives $0.7 \times 0.1$ in the denominator.

da-2026-da-48.approach: One call of \`fun\` is exactly one bubble-sort pass that returns the number of adjacent swaps it made. Every swap of an adjacent out-of-order pair removes exactly one inversion, and 5 passes are enough to sort 5 elements, so the printed total equals the number of inversions of the initial list.

steps.title: What one call of fun does
steps.body: \`fun(L, i)\` compares \`L[i]\` and \`L[i+1]\` for $i = 0, 1, \ldots, \text{len}(L)-2$, swaps them when \`L[i] > L[i+1]\` (the tuple assignment is a genuine swap), and adds 1 per swap. So \`fun(data)\` is one left-to-right bubble pass that returns its swap count. \`data\` is mutated in place, so the passes accumulate.

scene.caption: After pass 1 (5 bubbled to the end)

steps.title: Passes 4 and 5: no swaps
steps.body: The list is sorted, so both remaining calls return $0$. Final count $= 4+2+2+0+0 = 8$; the program prints **8**.

pitfalls: Thinking each call restarts from the original list — \`data\` is mutated in place.
Counting comparisons (4 per pass, 20 total) instead of swaps.
Stopping after the first pass (answer 4).
da-2026-da-48.verification: Inversion count (shortcut) and the explicit pass-by-pass trace both give $8$.

da-2026-da-49.approach: Simplify the formula first: the clause $\exists z \in X\,(t[P] = z[P])$ is always true (take $z = t$), so the query returns the tuples of $X$ whose $P$ value has at least one matching $Y$ tuple with $S > 1$ — a semi-join.

steps.title: The z-clause is a tautology
steps.body:
Since $t \in X$, choosing $z = t$ satisfies $t[P] = z[P]$. So the condition reduces to
$$t \in X \land \exists m \in Y\,(m[P] = t[P] \land m[S] > 1).$$

steps.title: Check each tuple of X against Y
steps.body:
- $t = (P1, Q1, R1)$: $Y$ has $(P1, 10)$ and $(P1, 15)$; $10 > 1$ ✓ → returned.
- $t = (P2, Q2, R2)$: $Y$ has $(P2, 20)$; $20 > 1$ ✓ → returned.
- $t = (P3, Q3, R2)$: the only match is $(P3, 1)$; $1 > 1$ is false ✗ → not returned.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: The result is $\{(P1,Q1,R1), (P2,Q2,R2)\}$. Two $Y$ tuples match P1, but $t$ ranges over $X$, so P1 is returned once. Answer: **2** (the official key accepts the range 2 to 3).

da-2026-da-49.shortcut: It is $X \ltimes \sigma_{S>1}(Y)$: $\sigma_{S>1}(Y)$ keeps P1, P1, P2; the $X$ tuples with P in $\{P1, P2\}$ number 2.
pitfalls: Counting P1 twice because it matches two $Y$ tuples — the result is a set of $X$ tuples.
Treating $m[S] > 1$ as $\ge 1$, which would wrongly include P3.
da-2026-da-49.verification: Equivalent SQL: \`SELECT * FROM X WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Y WHERE Y.P = X.P AND Y.S > 1)\` returns the P1 and P2 rows only.

da-2026-da-50.approach: The correlated subqueries count, for each row, how many balances are strictly larger and how many strictly smaller. Tabulate both counts per row and keep rows with (#larger) $\ge$ (#smaller).

steps.title: Meaning of the two subqueries
steps.body: For the outer row $A$: the left subquery counts rows $B$ with $B.\text{Balance} > A.\text{Balance}$ (strictly larger); the right counts rows $C$ with $C.\text{Balance} < A.\text{Balance}$ (strictly smaller). Equal balances count in neither.

steps.title: A1 and A2 (5000)
steps.body: Larger: 10000, 15000, 18000 → $3$. Smaller: none → $0$ (the other 5000 is equal, not smaller). $3 \ge 0$ ✓ for both A1 and A2.

steps.title: A4 (15000) and A5 (18000)
steps.body:
A4: larger $1$ (18000), smaller $3$ → $1 \ge 3$ ✗. A5: larger $0$, smaller $4$ → ✗.

Rows returned: A1, A2, A3 → **3**.

answer.value: The query returns **3** rows (A1, A2, A3)

da-2026-da-50.shortcut: The condition "#above $\ge$ #below" keeps the rows at or below the median balance (10000): A1, A2, A3.
pitfalls: Counting the equal 5000 as "smaller" for A1/A2 — the comparisons are strict.
Using $>$ instead of $\ge$ would drop A3 and give 2.
da-2026-da-50.verification: Each row's larger + smaller + equal (excluding itself) $= 4$: A1: $3+0+1$, A3: $2+2+0$, A4: $1+3+0$ ✓.

da-2026-da-51.approach: Apply the standard ER-to-relational mapping: one relation per strong entity (without the multivalued attribute), one relation per multivalued attribute, and a separate relation for an M:N relationship — total participation does not allow merging an M:N relationship into either side.

steps.title: Entities
steps.body:
$E1(\underline{A11}, A12, A13)$ — key $A11$, in 3NF.

$E2(\underline{A21}, A23)$ — the multivalued $A22$ cannot be stored in a single column (1NF), so it is removed from $E2$.

steps.title: Multivalued attribute A22
steps.body: $E2\_A22(\underline{A21, A22})$: one row per (entity, value) pair; the key is the whole schema, so it is in BCNF (hence 3NF).

steps.title: M:N relationship R12
steps.body: $R12(\underline{A11, A21})$. It cannot be merged into $E1$ or $E2$: in a merged table the key would be $(A11, A21)$ while $A11 \to A12, A13$ (or $A21 \to A23$) is a **partial dependency**, violating 2NF/3NF and duplicating $E1$ data for every partner. Total participation only says each entity has at least one partner — it does not make the relationship functional.

da-2026-da-51.shortcut: Entities (2) + multivalued attributes (1) + M:N relationships (1) $= 4$; total participation matters only for 1:1 / 1:N merging.
pitfalls: Merging the M:N relationship into an entity because participation is total — that creates partial dependencies.
Keeping $A22$ inside $E2$ (violates 1NF) and answering 3.
Merging $E1$, $E2$ and $R12$ into one table — key $(A11, A21)$ with partial dependencies.
da-2026-da-51.verification: Each relation's only non-trivial FDs have a superkey on the left: $A11 \to A12A13$ in $E1$, $A21 \to A23$ in $E2$; $E2\_A22$ and $R12$ are all-key. All four are in BCNF, so 3NF holds; no fewer relations avoid a partial dependency.

da-2026-da-52.approach: Use the identity $\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n (x_i - x_j)^2 = 2n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)^2$, so the given double sum fixes the sum of squared deviations directly.

steps.title: Prove the identity
steps.body:
Expand: $\sum_i\sum_j (x_i^2 + x_j^2 - 2x_ix_j) = n\sum_i x_i^2 + n\sum_j x_j^2 - 2\left(\sum_i x_i\right)\left(\sum_j x_j\right)$
$$= 2n\sum_i x_i^2 - 2(n\bar x)^2 = 2n\left(\sum_i x_i^2 - n\bar x^2\right) = 2n\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2.$$

steps.title: Use the given value
steps.body: $\frac{1}{2000}\sum_i\sum_j (x_i-x_j)^2 = 99 \Rightarrow \sum_i\sum_j (x_i-x_j)^2 = 99 \times 2000 = 198000$.

steps.title: Required value
steps.body: $\frac{1}{99}\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2 = \frac{990}{99} = 10$. (This is the sample variance $s^2$ with divisor $n - 1 = 99$.)

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor 2 in $2n$ (each unordered pair is counted twice) gives 20.
Using $n^2$ instead of $2n$ in the identity.
da-2026-da-52.verification: Tiny check of the identity: $x = (0, 2)$, $n = 2$: $\sum\sum(x_i-x_j)^2 = 4+4 = 8$; $2n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2 = 4(1+1) = 8$ ✓.

da-2026-da-53.approach: Compute the covariance through the tower property: $E[XY] = E[X\,E[Y\mid X]] = E[X^3] = 0$ by symmetry of $X$ about 0. Zero covariance (with positive variances) means zero correlation, even though $Y$ clearly depends on $X$.

steps.title: Conditional mean of Y
steps.body: The mean of $Uniform(a, b)$ is $\frac{a+b}{2}$, so $E[Y\mid X=x] = \frac{(x^2-0.1)+(x^2+0.1)}{2} = x^2$.

steps.title: E[X] and E[XY]
steps.body:
$E[X] = 0$ (Uniform$(-1,1)$ is symmetric about 0).

$E[XY] = E\big[X\,E[Y\mid X]\big] = E[X\cdot X^2] = E[X^3] = \int_{-1}^{1} \tfrac12 x^3\,dx = 0$ (odd integrand on a symmetric interval).

steps.title: Covariance
steps.body: $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = 0 - 0\cdot E[Y] = 0$.

steps.title: Correlation
steps.body:
Both variances are positive: $\text{Var}(X) = \frac{(1-(-1))^2}{12} = \frac13$, and $\text{Var}(Y) \ge E[\text{Var}(Y\mid X)] = \frac{0.2^2}{12} > 0$. Hence
$$\rho(X,Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\text{Var}(Y)}} = 0.$$

da-2026-da-53.shortcut: $E[Y\mid X] = X^2$ is an even function of a symmetric $X$, so $\text{Cov}(X, X^2) = E[X^3] = 0$ — the dependence is purely non-linear.
pitfalls: Concluding the correlation is non-zero because $Y$ depends on $X$ — correlation measures only linear association.
Forgetting to check that $\text{Var}(Y) > 0$ (otherwise the correlation would be undefined).
da-2026-da-53.verification: Symmetry: $(X, Y)$ and $(-X, Y)$ have the same joint distribution (the conditional law of $Y$ depends on $x^2$ only), so $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \text{Cov}(-X,Y) = -\text{Cov}(X,Y) \Rightarrow 0$.

da-2026-da-54.approach: Row 2 and column 3 share exactly one entry, $a_{23}$. Condition on it: given $a_{23}$, the other 4 entries of the row and the other 4 of the column are disjoint independent sets, each with a Binomial$(4, \tfrac12)$ sum.
concepts: Independence of disjoint sets of entries

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Row 2 = $a_{23}$ + 4 other entries; column 3 = $a_{23}$ + 4 other entries; these 8 other entries are distinct, so the two partial sums $R', C' \sim \text{Bin}(4, \tfrac12)$ are independent and independent of $a_{23}$. $P(\text{Bin}(4,\tfrac12) = k) = \binom4k/16$.

steps.title: Case a₂₃ = 1
steps.body: Need $R' = 2$ and $C' = 2$: $P = \frac12 \cdot \frac{\binom42}{16}\cdot\frac{\binom42}{16} = \frac12\cdot\frac{6}{16}\cdot\frac{6}{16} = \frac{36}{512}$.

steps.title: Case a₂₃ = 0
steps.body: Need $R' = 3$ and $C' = 3$: $P = \frac12 \cdot \frac{\binom43}{16}\cdot\frac{\binom43}{16} = \frac12\cdot\frac{4}{16}\cdot\frac{4}{16} = \frac{16}{512}$.

da-2026-da-54.shortcut: Count the 9 relevant bits: $a_{23}=1$: $6\cdot6 = 36$ patterns; $a_{23}=0$: $4\cdot4 = 16$ patterns; total $52/2^9 = 52/512 \approx 0.10$.
pitfalls: Treating the row sum and column sum as independent: $\left(\binom53/32\right)^2 = (10/32)^2 \approx 0.098$ — close, but the reasoning is wrong (they share $a_{23}$).
Forgetting one of the two cases for the shared entry.
da-2026-da-54.verification: Brute force over the $2^9 = 512$ patterns of the 9 cells in row 2 ∪ column 3 gives exactly 52 favourable patterns, i.e. $0.1016$.

da-2026-da-55.approach: $\max_{\lVert x\rVert=1} x^TAx$ of a symmetric matrix is its largest eigenvalue (Rayleigh quotient). $A = I - \frac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T$ is the orthogonal projection onto the complement of $\mathbf{1}$, whose eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$.

steps.title: A is a symmetric projection
steps.body:
$A^T = A$, and
$$A^2 = I - \tfrac2n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T + \tfrac{1}{n^2}\mathbf{1}(\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{1})\mathbf{1}^T = I - \tfrac2n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T + \tfrac{n}{n^2}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T = A,$$
using $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{1} = n$. An idempotent symmetric matrix has eigenvalues only $0$ or $1$.

steps.title: Find the eigenvalues explicitly
steps.body:
$A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} - \tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\cdot n = \mathbf 0$ → eigenvalue $0$ (once).

For any $v \perp \mathbf{1}$ ($\mathbf{1}^Tv = 0$): $Av = v$ → eigenvalue $1$, multiplicity $n - 1$.

steps.title: Rayleigh quotient maximum
steps.body: For symmetric $A$, $\max_{x^Tx=1} x^TAx = \lambda_{\max}(A) = 1$, attained by any unit vector with zero mean, e.g. $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0, \ldots, 0)^T$: $x^TAx = x^Tx - \frac1n(\mathbf{1}^Tx)^2 = 1 - 0 = 1$.

da-2026-da-55.shortcut: $x^TAx = x^Tx - \frac1n(\mathbf 1^Tx)^2 = 1 - \frac1n\big(\sum x_i\big)^2 \le 1$, with equality when $\sum x_i = 0$ (possible for $n \ge 2$).
pitfalls: Thinking the maximum depends on $n$ (e.g. $1 - \frac1n$, which is the value at a standard basis vector, not the maximum).
Picking the eigenvalue $0$ (eigenvector $\mathbf{1}$) — that is the minimum.
da-2026-da-55.verification: Two independent routes agree: the eigenvalue argument ($\lambda_{\max} = 1$) and the direct bound $x^TAx = 1 - \frac1n(\sum x_i)^2 \le 1$ with equality at a zero-sum unit vector.
